domains.title: Witness at Creation
domains.subtitle: Wisdom, Divination, and the Ifá Corpus
domains.lead: Ọrúnmìlà is the orixá of wisdom and the patron of Ifá, the divination system that reads human destiny against the patterns of the cosmos. Present at creation, he alone remembers how the world was founded. Kings consult him before they act; his priests, the babalawos, speak for him through sixteen palm nuts.

cards.name: Ifá Divination
cards.desc: Sixteen palm nuts and the divination chain reveal the odù that governs a situation.

cards.name: Sacred Knowledge
cards.desc: He remembers the verses, medicines, and sacrifices that restore cosmic balance.

cards.name: Witness of Creation
cards.desc: Only he saw the world being made; therefore only he can interpret its deepest laws.

cards.name: Babalawo
cards.desc: The father of secrets — the title of the priests who speak for him in divination.

mythology.lead: Ọrúnmìlà's mythology lives in the thousands of Ifá verses (òdù Ifá) that record his journeys, judgments, and interventions — wisdom's biography told as scripture.

myths.title: The Witness at the Foundation of the World
myths.text: According to Ifá tradition, Ọrúnmìlà was the only orixá present when Olódùmarè created the earth. He observed the placing of the rivers, the rising of the mountains, and the distribution of destinies, and the corpus never stops drawing authority from that attendance (Abimbola, Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus, 1976; Bascom, Ifa Divination, 1969). The other orishas received domains; Ọrúnmìlà received the memory of everything. Because he witnessed the beginning, he can trace any present trouble back to its origin and prescribe the sacrifice that will set it right. The Ifá verses return to this scene whenever authority is questioned, and it has silenced sceptics for centuries. The myth defines knowledge as witnessing rather than power: the one who watched the world being made became the one to whom the world turns when it forgets what it is for.

myths.title: Àgbọnnìrègún, the Medicine That Never Fails
myths.text: Before descending to earth, Ọrúnmìlà received from Olódùmarè the gift called àgbọnnìrègún — the sixteen sacred palm nuts and the science of reading them, glossed in the corpus as 'the medicine that never fails' (Bascom 1969; Idowu, 1962). The myth has a practical moral: the other orishas came down with powers over fire, water, and iron, but Ọrúnmìlà came down with a method. Wherever he travelled — and the verses send him wandering through every kind of settlement — he could answer any question put to him by casting the nuts and reciting the odù that fell. That is why the nuts are addressed with the respect due a founder, and why their loss ends a priest's career. The story makes divination a deliberate endowment, not an improvisation: heaven equipped its witness with the one tool the world would never stop needing.

myths.title: The Man Who Chose a Bad Head
myths.text: A celebrated òdù narrative tells of a man who, before birth, knelt impatiently in heaven and seized the first head Àjàlá the potter offered — a cracked, ill-fired orí. On earth his life collapsed: his farms failed, his wives left, his name soured. At last he consulted Ifá, performed the prescribed sacrifice, and in a dream journey returned to the house of Àjàlá, where he exchanged the ruined head for a sound one; he woke on earth a different man (Abimbola 1976; the Orí cycle of narratives). The story is the corpus's most beloved parable of hope: destiny chosen cannot be unchosen, but heaven keeps a pottery, and sacrifice is the road back to it. Ọrúnmìlà's role is never to mock the careless chooser — only to chart the road back.

myths.title: The Client Who Would Not Sacrifice
myths.text: Countless òdù verses end the same way: a person consults Ifá, receives a precise prescription — offer this, avoid that — and ignores it; ruin follows exactly as the odù said it would (Bascom 1969 catalogues the motif). Sometimes the refuser is a king who will not humble himself, sometimes a trader who counts the ẹbọ too dear. Ọrúnmìlà never punishes; the ignored counsel simply unfolds, the way an unread letter still contains its bad news. The motif is the corpus's pedagogy of practice: divination is not knowledge for its own sake but knowledge tied to an act. A verse unperformed is a door left shut, and a sacrifice owed is a debt the world always collects. The god of wisdom measures understanding the way a doctor measures recovery — not by what you heard, but by what you did.

lore.syncretism: Ọrúnmìlà travelled to the Americas as the patron of Ifá and the apex of Santería's religious hierarchy. In Cuba, babalawos of the Regla de Ifá initiate through a ceremony that makes them 'godfathers' of the oracle itself, and Catholic syncretism sometimes pairs him with Saint Francis of Assisi, whose humility and poverty invited the identification. In Brazil he is Orunmilá, less publicly prominent than in Cuba but foundational to the Casas de Ifá that preserve the palm-nut casting beside the cowrie oracle. In both countries the figure who witnessed creation ended up witnessing another creation: a religion reassembled in exile, with himself as its librarian.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ọrúnmìlà's legacy is the Ifá corpus itself — one of the largest bodies of African sacred poetry, inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity as the 'Ifa divination system'. His influence reaches into literature, psychology, and ethics: the idea that wisdom is not possession but practice, that destiny can be read but must be met with sacrifice, and that the future is a conversation rather than a sentence. Contemporary African philosophers and diaspora theologians return to him as a model of disciplined, compassionate knowledge — the sage whose authority rests entirely on having paid attention when the world was made.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ọrúnmìlà is the god who knows that knowing is not enough. He possesses the memory of creation, yet his work is not to dazzle humans with that memory but to guide them through the small, repeated acts — casting nuts, reciting verses, making sacrifice — that restore alignment.

In an information-saturated age, Ọrúnmìlà offers a different model of wisdom. It is not the accumulation of facts but the patience to hear what a pattern means. The babalawo does not predict the future like a fortune-teller; he reads the shape of a life against the oldest stories and suggests the practical step that will turn the current. To approach Ọrúnmìlà is to admit that you do not know enough to act alone — and that this admission is the beginning of intelligence.

lore.archaeology: The Ifá corpus is preserved orally and in manuscript form across Yoruba-speaking regions, with material evidence in the divination kit itself: carved palm nuts (ikin), brass ọpẹ̀lẹ̀ chains, and wooden divination trays (ọpọ́n Ifá) whose rims bear the face of Ẹṣù. Bascom's mid-century recordings and Abimbola's transcriptions fixed tens of thousands of verses in writing for the first time. Diaspora collections hold beaded necklaces, iron staffs, and the palm-nut pouches of working babalawos in Havana and Bahia — instruments of a scripture whose primary medium remains the trained and consecrated memory.
